This notebook checks the storm surge exposure and sensitivity indicators and
the choices behind `calc_storm_surge_exposure()` and
`calc_storm_surge_sensitivity()`. The source data is the Muis et al. (2023)
CMIP6 storm surge dataset at the 10-year return period (RP10), with 4
HighResMIP models kept separate through preprocessing.

Exposure is the worst-case projected percent change at the nearest coastal
station, with CMCC-CM2-VHR4 excluded. Sensitivity is the 4-model mean
reference-period (1985-2014) surge level. Both are discounted by a joint
distance-to-coast and low-elevation weight. The sections below work through
each of those choices.

The correlation work at the end (Spearman heatmap, flagged pairs, jackknife by
dropping one indicator) follows the pattern in Caitlin's
`Explore/vulnerability_sensitivity_analysis.Rmd`, applied here at the
coastal-component level rather than across the full vulnerability index.

# Design rationale

This section explains why `calc_storm_surge_exposure()` and
`calc_storm_surge_sensitivity()` are built the way they are. The function
docstrings are kept short and point here. Each choice is worked through in the
sections further down.

## Exposure uses the worst-case model, with CMCC-CM2-VHR4 excluded

Exposure is meant to capture the largest projected change at each station, so
we take the worst case across the 4 models rather than an average. The worst
case is the largest percent change from the reference period to the future
period.

CMCC-CM2-VHR4 is left out of that pool. Muis et al. (2023) flag it as their
most biased model at RP100 (0.14 m mean bias), and it is biased high at RP10
too. Across all CONUS stations its median percent change is +23.4%, against
-0.5% to +2.5% for the other three models, and its max is +182.5% against 28
to 46% for the rest. The bias is worst on the Pacific coast, where the
reference surge level is low so a fixed bias turns into a large percent change.
Keeping CMCC in and switching to a mean of all 4 models breaks the ranking.
The rank correlation against current production drops to about 0.21.

## Sensitivity uses the 4-model mean, with no model excluded

The reference period (1985-2014) is a fixed historical window that has already
happened. There is no future worst case to worry about here, only the
estimation error each model has around the one real historical value, and a
multi-model mean averages those errors out. We did not use the max
reference-period level because the models it picks do not line up with the
models the exposure worst case picks. Using different models for sensitivity
and exposure seems more wrong than using the mean for sensitivity and the max
for exposure.

We do not exclude CMCC-CM2-VHR4 from the sensitivity mean. Its bias shows up in
the future-vs-reference change, not in the reference level itself, so it does
not pull the mean the way it would for exposure.

## Both indicators are weighted by distance to the coast and by elevation

The raw surge value comes from the nearest offshore Muis station, assigned by a
nearest-neighbor join. It is a stand-in for conditions at the water supply, not
a measurement there, so we discount it by how close the water supply actually
is to the coast and how low its elevation is. The weight is
`sqrt((dist_weight^2 + elev_weight^2) / 2)`. The elevation term is anchored to
the 10 m Low Elevation Coastal Zone threshold (McGranahan et al. 2007) rather
than the highest site elevation in the data, so the scale does not shift when
the set of water supplies changes.

We use an RMS blend so one term can partly make up for the other. An earlier
version multiplied the two weights together, which zeroed out 180 of 347
sites, including many that were well within 250 m of the coast.

# Setup

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
```

```{r}
source("setup.R")
mapviewOptions(fgb = FALSE)

EXPOSURE_COLOR    <- "#5B8C6E"
SENSITIVITY_COLOR <- "#7C6FAD"
pal <- colorRampPalette(c("green", "yellow", "red"))

minmax_norm <- function(x) {
  x <- as.numeric(x)
  rng <- range(x, na.rm = TRUE)
  if (!is.finite(rng[1]) || rng[2] == rng[1]) return(rep(NA_real_, length(x)))
  (x - rng[1]) / (rng[2] - rng[1])
}

# Slopegraph of percentile rank under two methods. One line per water supply,
# left point = rank under method a, right point = rank under method b, colored
# by whether the site moved up, down, or held (within 2 points).
rank_slopegraph <- function(df, rank_a, rank_b, label_a, label_b, title) {
  d <- df %>%
    dplyr::mutate(.a = {{ rank_a }}, .b = {{ rank_b }}) %>%
    dplyr::filter(!is.na(.a), !is.na(.b)) %>%
    dplyr::mutate(
      direction = dplyr::case_when(.b - .a > 2 ~ "moved up",
                                   .b - .a < -2 ~ "moved down",
                                   TRUE ~ "held"),
      tip = paste0(wsd_source_id, "<br>", park_name,
                   "<br>", label_a, ": ", round(.a, 1),
                   "<br>", label_b, ": ", round(.b, 1))
    )

  long <- dplyr::bind_rows(
    d %>% dplyr::transmute(wsd_source_id, direction, tip, x = label_a, rank = .a),
    d %>% dplyr::transmute(wsd_source_id, direction, tip, x = label_b, rank = .b)
  ) %>%
    dplyr::mutate(x = factor(x, levels = c(label_a, label_b)))

  p <- ggplot(long, aes(x, rank, group = wsd_source_id, color = direction, text = tip)) +
    geom_line(alpha = 0.4) +
    geom_point(size = 1, alpha = 0.6) +
    scale_color_manual(values = c("moved up" = "#B2182B", "moved down" = "#2166AC", "held" = "grey70")) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
    labs(title = title, x = NULL, y = "Percentile rank", color = NULL)

  plotly::ggplotly(p, tooltip = "text")
}
```

# Load data

```{r}
water_supplies <- get_wsd(rapid = TRUE)

storm_surge_stations_path <- here("data", "rapid", "inputs", "storm_surge", "storm_surge_RP10_muis_2023.gpkg")
coast_geometry_path <- here("data", "rapid", "inputs", "coast_comp", "coastal_site_geometry.csv")

# Last exposure output before this round of changes (pre-RMS weighting, RP100,
# no CMCC exclusion, worst-case by absolute change). Used only for the
# old-vs-new exposure comparison; that comparison bundles several changes at
# once, and the sections below isolate the CMCC exclusion on its own.
old_exposure <- readr::read_csv(
  here("data", "rapid", "outputs", "storm_surge_exposure_2026-08-13.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

# Other coastal-component indicators, most recent saved output of each
swi_exposure <- readr::read_csv(
  here("data", "rapid", "outputs", "swi_exposure_2026-08-13.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

inundation_exposure <- readr::read_csv(
  here("data", "rapid", "outputs", "inundation_exposure_2026-08-13.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
) %>%
  filter(buffer_km == 4)

inundation_sensitivity <- readr::read_csv(
  here("data", "rapid", "outputs", "inundation_sensitivity_2026-03-31.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
# Current production exposure and sensitivity, computed live from the
# processed RP10 station gpkg (not the raw NetCDFs), so this is fast.
new_exposure <- calc_storm_surge_exposure(
  water_supplies = water_supplies,
  storm_surge_stations = storm_surge_stations_path,
  coast_geometry = coast_geometry_path,
  save = FALSE,
  verbose = FALSE
)

new_sensitivity <- calc_storm_surge_sensitivity(
  water_supplies = water_supplies,
  storm_surge_stations = storm_surge_stations_path,
  coast_geometry = coast_geometry_path,
  save = FALSE,
  verbose = FALSE
)

# GRSA_WS_001_01 / GRSA_WS_002_01 are known duplicate wsd_source_id values in
# the source Excel database (see CLAUDE.md, Known Data Issues); dedupe so
# downstream joins stay one row per water supply. ncdf4::ncvar_get() also tags
# values with a leftover "array"/dim attribute that breaks mapview() and
# case_when(); as.numeric() strips it. Repeat both after every live calc call.
new_exposure <- new_exposure %>%
  distinct(wsd_source_id, .keep_all = TRUE) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), as.numeric))

new_sensitivity <- new_sensitivity %>%
  distinct(wsd_source_id, .keep_all = TRUE) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), as.numeric))
```

# TLDR

Current production storm surge exposure and sensitivity, and how the two
relate to each other. The design choices behind them:

| Choice | Effect |
|---|---|
| Exposure is the worst-case model by percent change | Captures the largest projected change at each station instead of pulling it toward the ensemble center. |
| CMCC-CM2-VHR4 is excluded from the exposure pool | Drops a nationally biased-high model that otherwise wins worst-case almost everywhere once the criterion is percent change. |
| Sensitivity is the 4-model mean of the reference level | The reference period already happened, so there is no future worst case, only per-model estimation error, which a mean averages down. |
| RMS distance + elevation weight, elevation capped at 10 m | Discounts the offshore station value by how coastal and how low the water supply is. RMS lets one term partly cover for the other so the elevation cap does not zero out sites right on the coast. |

## Combined exposure and sensitivity

```{r}
tldr_exp_sen <- new_exposure %>%
  select(wsd_source_id, park_unit, park_name, norm_exposure = norm_surge_pct_change_max) %>%
  inner_join(
    new_sensitivity %>% select(wsd_source_id, norm_sensitivity = norm_surge_reference_m),
    by = "wsd_source_id"
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(norm_exposure), !is.na(norm_sensitivity)) %>%
  mutate(combined_raw = sqrt(norm_exposure^2 + norm_sensitivity^2),
         combined_norm = minmax_norm(combined_raw))

tldr_combined_sf <- water_supplies %>%
  select(wsd_source_id) %>%
  inner_join(tldr_exp_sen, by = "wsd_source_id")

mapview(tldr_combined_sf, zcol = "combined_norm", col.regions = pal,
        layer.name = "Exposure + sensitivity, combined (norm)")
```

The combined score is the Euclidean distance of the two normalized indicators,
re-normalized 0-1. Exposure and sensitivity are only weakly correlated (see
"Correlation between exposure and sensitivity" below), so combining them keeps
information that either one alone would miss.

# Updated storm surge exposure

Previous exposure output against current production. The previous output
predates the RMS weighting, used RP100, kept all 4 models, and picked the
worst case by absolute change rather than percent change, so this comparison
bundles several changes at once. The section below it isolates the CMCC
exclusion on its own. Shown as normalized score and percentile rank, so
neither scale is left implicit.

```{r}
old_sf <- water_supplies %>%
  select(wsd_source_id) %>%
  inner_join(old_exposure, by = "wsd_source_id") %>%
  filter(!is.na(norm_surge_pct_change_max))

new_sf <- water_supplies %>%
  select(wsd_source_id) %>%
  inner_join(new_exposure, by = "wsd_source_id") %>%
  filter(!is.na(norm_surge_pct_change_max))

old_popup <- leafpop::popupTable(st_drop_geometry(old_sf) %>%
                                    select(wsd_source_id, park_name,

new_popup <- leafpop::popupTable(st_drop_geometry(new_sf) %>%
                                    select(wsd_source_id, park_name,
                                           raw_surge_pct_change_max,
                                           norm_surge_pct_change_max,
                                           rank_surge_pct_change_max))

m_old_norm <- mapview(old_sf, zcol = "norm_surge_pct_change_max", col.regions = pal,
                      layer.name = "Previous exposure, norm", popup = old_popup)

m_new_norm <- mapview(new_sf, zcol = "norm_surge_pct_change_max", col.regions = pal,
                      layer.name = "Current exposure, norm", popup = new_popup)

m_old_rank <- mapview(old_sf, zcol = "rank_surge_pct_change_max", col.regions = pal,
                      layer.name = "Previous exposure, rank", popup = old_popup)

m_new_rank <- mapview(new_sf, zcol = "rank_surge_pct_change_max", col.regions = pal,
                      layer.name = "Current exposure, rank", popup = new_popup)

leafsync::sync(m_old_norm, m_new_norm, m_old_rank, m_new_rank, ncol = 2)
```

## Previous vs. current: rank movement

```{r}
rank_compare <- old_exposure %>%
  select(wsd_source_id, park_unit, park_name,
         rank_old = rank_surge_pct_change_max) %>%
  inner_join(
    new_exposure %>% select(wsd_source_id, rank_new = rank_surge_pct_change_max),
    by = "wsd_source_id"
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(rank_old), !is.na(rank_new))

rank_slopegraph(rank_compare, rank_old, rank_new,
                "Previous", "Current",
                "Storm surge exposure percentile rank: previous vs. current")
```

Point Reyes (PORE) is the clearest mover. Every PORE water supply jumps from a
low single-digit percent change to a much higher one. That shift comes from
CMCC-CM2-VHR4, which wins the worst-case slot at all of PORE's nearest
stations once the criterion is percent change. The next section isolates that
model.

# What if CMCC-CM2-VHR4 is excluded from the worst-case model pool?

Muis et al. (2023) flag CMCC-CM2-VHR4 as their most biased ensemble member,
worst at the RP100 return period ("a higher mean bias than other models,
especially for the 100-year return period with a 0.14 m bias"). It is a fully
coupled ocean-atmosphere model, not the atmosphere-only member
(`HadGEM3-GC31-HM-SST`), so the bias is not an atmosphere-only artifact.

## Per-model percent-change distributions, all CONUS stations

If CMCC-CM2-VHR4 is biased high nationally, and not just at one outlier
station, switching the worst-case criterion to percent change would make it
win almost everywhere. That produces a floor-level shift rather than a few
isolated outliers. Below is the density of `(future_mean - reference_mean) /
reference_mean * 100` for each of the 4 models at every CONUS station, plus
the per-station mean across all 4 models (dashed).

```{r}
# One row per station per model, so each model's percent-change distribution
# can be pulled out separately.
stations_all <- sf::st_read(storm_surge_stations_path, quiet = TRUE) %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), as.numeric)) %>%
  mutate(pct_change = (future_mean - reference_mean) / reference_mean * 100)

station_mean <- stations_all %>%
  group_by(station_idx) %>%
  summarize(pct_change = mean(pct_change, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(model = "Mean of 4 models")

dist_df <- bind_rows(
  stations_all %>% select(model, pct_change),
  station_mean %>% select(model, pct_change)
)

model_colors <- c(
  "CMCC-CM2-VHR4"       = "#E76F51",
  "EC-Earth3P-HR"       = "#2A9D8F",
  "HadGEM3-GC31-HM"     = "#264653",
  "HadGEM3-GC31-HM-SST" = "#8AB17D",
  "Mean of 4 models"    = "black"
)
model_linewidths <- c(
  "CMCC-CM2-VHR4"       = 0.7, "EC-Earth3P-HR"   = 0.7,
  "HadGEM3-GC31-HM"     = 0.7, "HadGEM3-GC31-HM-SST" = 0.7,
  "Mean of 4 models"    = 1.3
)
model_linetypes <- c(
  "CMCC-CM2-VHR4"       = "solid", "EC-Earth3P-HR"   = "solid",
  "HadGEM3-GC31-HM"     = "solid", "HadGEM3-GC31-HM-SST" = "solid",
  "Mean of 4 models"    = "dashed"
)

ggplot(dist_df %>% filter(is.finite(pct_change)),
      aes(pct_change, color = model, linewidth = model, linetype = model)) +
  geom_density() +
  scale_color_manual(values = model_colors) +
  scale_linewidth_manual(values = model_linewidths, guide = "none") +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = model_linetypes, guide = "none") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-60, 200)) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  labs(title = "CONUS storm surge RP10: percent change by model, reference 1985-2014 to future 2021-2050",
       x = "% change", y = "Density", color = NULL)
```

```{r}
stations_all %>%
  group_by(model) %>%
  summarize(min = min(pct_change, na.rm = TRUE),
            p05 = quantile(pct_change, .05, na.rm = TRUE),
            median = median(pct_change, na.rm = TRUE),
            p95 = quantile(pct_change, .95, na.rm = TRUE),
            max = max(pct_change, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  knitr::kable(digits = 1, caption = "Percent-change distribution by model, all CONUS stations, RP10 (x-axis above is trimmed to -60/200; CMCC's max extends further right)")
```

CMCC-CM2-VHR4 is the outlier. Its median percent change is +23.4% against
-0.5% to +2.5% for the other three, and its max is +182.5% against 28 to 46%
for the rest. This holds at RP10, same pattern as the original RP100 finding
at a smaller magnitude. It is not a fluke at one Pacific station. It is a
nationally biased-high model, and switching the worst-case criterion to
percent change (which hunts for the largest relative jump) makes it the winner
almost everywhere.

## Worst-case with and without CMCC-CM2-VHR4

`calc_storm_surge_exposure_filtered()` is a parameterized copy of production's
logic with one added `filter(!model %in% exclude_models)` step before the
per-station worst-case reduction. It builds both sides of the comparison here,
all 4 models and CMCC-excluded, independently of what production does by
default (production already excludes CMCC-CM2-VHR4).

```{r}
calc_storm_surge_exposure_filtered <- function(water_supplies,
                                               storm_surge_stations,
                                               coast_geometry,
                                               exclude_models = character(0)) {
  if (is.character(storm_surge_stations)) {
    storm_surge_stations <- sf::st_read(storm_surge_stations, quiet = TRUE)
  }

  prepped_stations <- storm_surge_stations %>%
    filter(!model %in% exclude_models) %>%
    group_by(station_idx) %>%
    mutate(raw_surge_change_max = future_mean - reference_mean,
           raw_surge_pct_change_max = ((future_mean - reference_mean) / reference_mean) * 100) %>%
    slice_max(raw_surge_pct_change_max, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) %>%
    ungroup() %>%
    select(station_idx, model, raw_surge_change_max, raw_surge_pct_change_max, lat, lon)

  ws_proj <- sf::st_transform(water_supplies, 5070)
  stations_proj <- sf::st_transform(prepped_stations, 5070)

  nn_result <- nngeo::st_nn(ws_proj, stations_proj, k = 1, returnDist = TRUE, progress = FALSE)
  nn_idx <- unlist(nn_result$nn)
  nn_dist <- unlist(nn_result$dist)

  results <- water_supplies %>%
    sf::st_drop_geometry() %>%
    dplyr::select(wsd_source_id, park_unit, park_name) %>%
    dplyr::mutate(nn_dist_m = nn_dist,
                  raw_surge_change_max = stations_proj$raw_surge_change_max[nn_idx],
                  raw_surge_pct_change_max = stations_proj$raw_surge_pct_change_max[nn_idx]) %>%
    dplyr::mutate(raw_surge_change_max = dplyr::if_else(nn_dist_m > 50000, NA_real_, raw_surge_change_max),
                  raw_surge_pct_change_max = dplyr::if_else(nn_dist_m > 50000, NA_real_, raw_surge_pct_change_max)) %>%
    dplyr::select(-nn_dist_m)

  coast_geometry_df <- readr::read_csv(coast_geometry, show_col_types = FALSE)

  results <- results %>%
    dplyr::left_join(coast_geometry_df, by = c("wsd_source_id", "park_unit", "park_name")) %>%
    mutate(raw_surge_change_max = dplyr::if_else(coast_dist_m > 50000, NA_real_, raw_surge_change_max))

  lecz_cap_m <- 10

  results <- results %>%
    dplyr::mutate(
      coast_weight = pmax(0, 1 - pmin(coast_dist_m, 50000) / 50000),
      elev_weight = 1 - pmin(pmax(coast_elev_m, 0) / lecz_cap_m, 1),
      joint_weight = sqrt((coast_weight^2 + elev_weight^2) / 2),
      raw_surge_change_max = raw_surge_change_max * joint_weight,
      raw_surge_pct_change_max = raw_surge_pct_change_max * joint_weight) %>%
    dplyr::select(-c(coast_dist_m, coast_weight, elev_weight, joint_weight))

  results %>%
    add_standardized_indicators("raw_surge_change_max", invert = FALSE) %>%
    add_standardized_indicators("raw_surge_pct_change_max", invert = FALSE)
}

all4_exposure <- calc_storm_surge_exposure_filtered(
  water_supplies = water_supplies,
  storm_surge_stations = storm_surge_stations_path,
  coast_geometry = coast_geometry_path,
  exclude_models = character(0)
) %>%
  distinct(wsd_source_id, .keep_all = TRUE) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), as.numeric))

no_cmcc_exposure <- calc_storm_surge_exposure_filtered(
  water_supplies = water_supplies,
  storm_surge_stations = storm_surge_stations_path,
  coast_geometry = coast_geometry_path,
  exclude_models = "CMCC-CM2-VHR4"
) %>%
  distinct(wsd_source_id, .keep_all = TRUE) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), as.numeric))
```

```{r}
# Sanity check: no_cmcc_exposure is the standalone CMCC-excluded reimplementation
# above. new_exposure is production's own calc_storm_surge_exposure(), which also
# excludes CMCC-CM2-VHR4 by default. They should agree almost exactly.
sanity_check <- no_cmcc_exposure %>%
  select(wsd_source_id, norm_standalone = norm_surge_pct_change_max) %>%
  inner_join(new_exposure %>% select(wsd_source_id, norm_production = norm_surge_pct_change_max),
             by = "wsd_source_id") %>%
  filter(!is.na(norm_standalone), !is.na(norm_production))

sanity_rho <- cor(sanity_check$norm_standalone, sanity_check$norm_production,
                  method = "spearman", use = "pairwise.complete.obs")

cat("Standalone CMCC-excluded reimplementation vs. production new_exposure, Spearman rho:",
    round(sanity_rho, 4), "(n =", nrow(sanity_check), ", expected ~1.0)\n")
```

## All 4 models vs. CMCC-excluded: rank movement

```{r}
rank_compare_cmcc <- all4_exposure %>%
  select(wsd_source_id, park_unit, park_name, rank_all4 = rank_surge_pct_change_max) %>%
  inner_join(
    no_cmcc_exposure %>% select(wsd_source_id, rank_nocmcc = rank_surge_pct_change_max),
    by = "wsd_source_id"
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(rank_all4), !is.na(rank_nocmcc))

rank_slopegraph(rank_compare_cmcc, rank_all4, rank_nocmcc,
                "All 4 models", "CMCC excluded",
                "Storm surge exposure percentile rank: all 4 models vs. CMCC-CM2-VHR4 excluded")
```

Excluding CMCC-CM2-VHR4 changes which model wins worst-case at a station, not
whether the station has a valid value, so coverage is identical under both.
The sites that drop are the ones where CMCC was winning worst-case on a large
relative jump, concentrated on the Pacific coast. The standalone
reimplementation here and production's own output agree almost exactly (see the
sanity check above).

# Worst-case vs. averaging

We also looked at a median-of-4 and a mean-of-4 in place of the worst-case
selection. Neither was adopted for exposure. A mean of all 4 models including
CMCC-CM2-VHR4 breaks the ranking (rank correlation about 0.21 against current
production) because CMCC's bias is geographically uneven. It inflates
Pacific-coast percent change far more than Gulf or Atlantic, since the Pacific
reference surge level is roughly three times lower, so the same absolute bias
becomes a much larger percent change. That would push several Pacific sites
from the bottom of the ranking to the top. Exposure is meant to capture the
genuine biggest-mover risk at each station, not smooth it out, so worst-case
is kept.

Sensitivity is the opposite case. The reference period (1985-2014) has already
happened, so there is no future worst case to capture, only per-model
estimation error around one real historical value. A multi-model mean is the
standard way to reduce that error, so sensitivity uses the 4-model mean.
CMCC-CM2-VHR4 stays in that mean because its bias is in the future-vs-reference
change, not in the reference level.

Both choices are reflected in `src/rapid/calc_storm_surge_exposure.R`,
`src/rapid/calc_storm_surge_sensitivity.R`, and `rapid_workflow.Rmd`.

# Correlation between exposure and sensitivity

```{r}
exp_sen <- new_exposure %>%
  select(wsd_source_id, park_unit, park_name,
         norm_exposure = norm_surge_pct_change_max) %>%
  inner_join(
    new_sensitivity %>% select(wsd_source_id, norm_sensitivity = norm_surge_reference_m),
    by = "wsd_source_id"
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(norm_exposure), !is.na(norm_sensitivity))

exp_sen_rho <- cor(exp_sen$norm_exposure, exp_sen$norm_sensitivity,
                   method = "spearman", use = "pairwise.complete.obs")

p <- ggplot(exp_sen, aes(norm_exposure, norm_sensitivity,
                         text = paste0(wsd_source_id, "<br>", park_name))) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, color = SENSITIVITY_COLOR) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  labs(title = paste0("Storm surge exposure vs. sensitivity (n = ", nrow(exp_sen),
                      ", Spearman rho = ", round(exp_sen_rho, 3), ")"),
       x = "Exposure (norm)", y = "Sensitivity (norm)")

plotly::ggplotly(p, tooltip = "text")
```

Some positive correlation is structural. Both indicators use the same
nearest-station assignment and the same distance and elevation weighting. A low
rho on top of that means the two are not redundant. A site can face a modest
projected future change in surge while already sitting on a high present-day
baseline, or the reverse. The combined score in the TLDR keeps both.

# Correlations with the other coastal indicators

```{r}
coastal_join <- new_exposure %>%
  select(wsd_source_id, park_unit, park_name,
         storm_surge_exp = norm_surge_pct_change_max) %>%
  left_join(new_sensitivity %>% select(wsd_source_id, storm_surge_sen = norm_surge_reference_m),
           by = "wsd_source_id") %>%
  left_join(swi_exposure %>% select(wsd_source_id, swi_exp = norm_swi_migration),
           by = "wsd_source_id") %>%
  left_join(inundation_exposure %>% select(wsd_source_id, inundation_exp = norm_coverage_pct_proj),
           by = "wsd_source_id") %>%
  left_join(inundation_sensitivity %>% select(wsd_source_id, inundation_sen = norm_shore_dist_m),
           by = "wsd_source_id")
```

## Exposure correlations

```{r}
exp_cols <- c("storm_surge_exp", "swi_exp", "inundation_exp")
exp_mat <- cor(coastal_join[, exp_cols], use = "pairwise.complete.obs", method = "spearman")

exp_long <- as.data.frame(as.table(exp_mat)) %>%
  rename(var1 = Var1, var2 = Var2, correlation = Freq)

ggplot(exp_long, aes(var1, var2, fill = correlation)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(correlation, 2)), size = 4) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = SENSITIVITY_COLOR, mid = "white", high = EXPOSURE_COLOR,
                        midpoint = 0, limits = c(-1, 1)) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)) +
  labs(title = "Coastal exposure indicator correlation matrix (Spearman)",
       x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = expression(rho))
```

```{r}
exp_long %>%
  filter(as.character(var1) < as.character(var2)) %>%
  arrange(desc(abs(correlation))) %>%
  knitr::kable(digits = 3, caption = "Exposure indicator pairs, sorted by |rho|")
```

## Sensitivity correlations

```{r}
sen_cols <- c("storm_surge_sen", "inundation_sen")
sen_pairs <- coastal_join %>% filter(!is.na(storm_surge_sen), !is.na(inundation_sen))
sen_rho <- cor(sen_pairs$storm_surge_sen, sen_pairs$inundation_sen,
              method = "spearman", use = "pairwise.complete.obs")

p <- ggplot(sen_pairs, aes(storm_surge_sen, inundation_sen,
                           text = paste0(wsd_source_id, "<br>", park_name))) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, color = SENSITIVITY_COLOR) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  labs(title = paste0("Storm surge sensitivity vs. inundation sensitivity (n = ", nrow(sen_pairs),
                      ", Spearman rho = ", round(sen_rho, 3), ")"),
       x = "Storm surge sensitivity (norm)", y = "Inundation sensitivity: shore distance (norm)")

plotly::ggplotly(p, tooltip = "text")
```

Only two present-day coastal sensitivity indicators currently exist: storm
surge reference-period surge height, and inundation sensitivity's
distance-to-shore. So this is a single pairwise comparison rather than a
matrix. Both are proxies for how coastal a site is, in different ways.
`inundation_sen` is a direct distance measurement. `storm_surge_sen` is a
distance-and-elevation-weighted surge magnitude. A positive correlation here
is expected on construction grounds, not necessarily evidence of redundancy.

## How the combined coastal exposure indicator changes when jackknifed

Mirrors `factor_exp_slr` (inundation + SWI + storm surge, Euclidean
combination) from Caitlin's `vulnerability_sensitivity_analysis.Rmd`
Section 4b/5c, using the storm surge exposure value from this notebook.

```{r}
slr_full <- coastal_join %>%
  filter(!is.na(storm_surge_exp) | !is.na(swi_exp) | !is.na(inundation_exp))

slr_mat <- as.matrix(slr_full[, exp_cols])
full_score <- minmax_norm(sqrt(rowSums(slr_mat^2, na.rm = TRUE)))

jackknife_indicators <- function(mat, full_score, indicator_cols) {
  purrr::map_dfr(indicator_cols, function(drop) {
    remaining <- setdiff(indicator_cols, drop)
    dropped_score <- if (length(remaining) == 1) {
      minmax_norm(abs(mat[, remaining]))
    } else {
      minmax_norm(sqrt(rowSums(mat[, remaining, drop = FALSE]^2, na.rm = TRUE)))
    }
    tibble::tibble(
      indicator_dropped = drop,
      rank_correlation = cor(full_score, dropped_score, method = "spearman", use = "pairwise.complete.obs"),
      mean_abs_delta = mean(abs(full_score - dropped_score), na.rm = TRUE)
    )
  }) %>%
    mutate(importance = round(1 - rank_correlation, 4)) %>%
    arrange(desc(importance))
}

coastal_exp_importance <- jackknife_indicators(slr_mat, full_score, exp_cols)

knitr::kable(coastal_exp_importance, digits = 3,
            caption = "Jackknife importance of each coastal exposure indicator (1 - rank correlation with the full combined score when dropped)")
```

```{r}
ggplot(coastal_exp_importance, aes(x = reorder(indicator_dropped, importance), y = importance)) +
  geom_col(fill = EXPOSURE_COLOR) +
  coord_flip() +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  labs(title = "Coastal exposure: importance of each indicator to the combined score",
       x = NULL, y = "Importance (1 - rank correlation when dropped)")
```

The higher an indicator's importance here, the more the combined coastal
exposure score depends on that indicator being present rather than inferred
from the other two. A low-importance indicator (high rank correlation when
dropped) is one whose information is already largely captured by the remaining
indicators. Euclidean combination is conjunctive: a high combined score
requires all three inputs to be high at once, not just one (see Caitlin's
Section 5c). So an indicator with structurally different missingness or
magnitude from the other two is expected to show up as more important here.
Storm surge is Gulf/Atlantic with limited Pacific coverage via Muis stations,
while SWI and inundation have broader coastal coverage. That is a
domain-coverage effect, not a sign storm surge carries more real information.

# Complete coastal component score

The sections above build each coastal indicator's exposure and sensitivity
scores independently. This section mixes them the way
`calc_vulnerability_index()` mixes indicators into a factor and factors into a
component. Within each side (exposure, sensitivity) it takes the Euclidean
distance across the normalized indicators in `exp_cols` / `sen_cols` above,
re-normalized 0-1. That is the same pattern production uses for its own
multi-indicator factors (`factor_exp_runoff`, `factor_sen_demand`, etc., see
`src/rapid/calc_vulnerability_index.R`). The two factor scores then combine the
way `EXPOSURE` and `SENSITIVITY` combine into `VULNERABILITY`: a missing side
is excluded from the sum rather than zero-filled (`na.rm = TRUE`), matching
production's handling of domain-limited indicators like storm surge.

Production's actual `factor_exp_slr` / `factor_sen_slr` are still
single-indicator SLR-inundation passthroughs, with no storm surge or SWI
folded in yet (see lines 123-142 of `calc_vulnerability_index.R`). This rebuilds
what those factors would look like with storm surge and SWI added, per
Caitlin's `vulnerability_sensitivity_analysis.Rmd` `factor_exp_slr` redesign.

```{r}
coastal_scored <- coastal_join %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  mutate(
    coastal_exposure_raw = if (all(is.na(c_across(all_of(exp_cols))))) {
      NA_real_
    } else {
      sqrt(sum(c_across(all_of(exp_cols))^2, na.rm = TRUE))
    },
    coastal_sensitivity_raw = if (all(is.na(c_across(all_of(sen_cols))))) {
      NA_real_
    } else {
      sqrt(sum(c_across(all_of(sen_cols))^2, na.rm = TRUE))
    }
  ) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(
    coastal_exposure_factor    = minmax_norm(coastal_exposure_raw),
    coastal_sensitivity_factor = minmax_norm(coastal_sensitivity_raw),
    coastal_component_raw = case_when(
      is.na(coastal_exposure_factor) & is.na(coastal_sensitivity_factor) ~ NA_real_,
      is.na(coastal_exposure_factor) ~ coastal_sensitivity_factor,
      is.na(coastal_sensitivity_factor) ~ coastal_exposure_factor,
      TRUE ~ sqrt(coastal_exposure_factor^2 + coastal_sensitivity_factor^2)
    ),
    coastal_component_norm = minmax_norm(coastal_component_raw)
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(coastal_component_norm))

coastal_full_sf <- water_supplies %>%
  select(wsd_source_id) %>%
  inner_join(coastal_scored, by = "wsd_source_id")

cat("Water supplies with a computable coastal component score:", nrow(coastal_full_sf), "\n")
```

## Popup: per-site indicator contributions

Mirrors the app's "Generate Report" factor bar chart (`rapid_app/app.R`,
`generate_report_btn` handler). One bar per normalized indicator feeding the
combined score, colored by exposure (green) vs. sensitivity (purple), instead
of a plain attribute table. Rendered with `leafpop::popupGraph()`, which
embeds a small PNG of each site's own plot in its popup.

```{r}
indicator_labels <- c(
  storm_surge_exp = "Storm Surge\n(Exp)",
  swi_exp         = "SWI\n(Exp)",
  inundation_exp  = "SLR Inun.\n(Exp)",
  storm_surge_sen = "Storm Surge\n(Sen)",
  inundation_sen  = "SLR Inun.\n(Sen)"
)

make_contribution_plot <- function(wsd_source_id, coastal_component_norm,
                                    storm_surge_exp, swi_exp, inundation_exp,
                                    storm_surge_sen, inundation_sen, ...) {
  vals <- c(storm_surge_exp = storm_surge_exp, swi_exp = swi_exp,
            inundation_exp = inundation_exp, storm_surge_sen = storm_surge_sen,
            inundation_sen = inundation_sen)

  plot_df <- tibble::tibble(
    indicator = factor(indicator_labels[names(vals)], levels = indicator_labels),
    score     = as.numeric(vals),
    side      = rep(c("Exposure", "Sensitivity"), c(3, 2))
  ) %>%
    filter(!is.na(score))

  ggplot(plot_df, aes(indicator, score, fill = side)) +
    geom_col(width = 0.6) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c(Exposure = EXPOSURE_COLOR, Sensitivity = SENSITIVITY_COLOR),
                       guide = "none") +
    scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05))) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = "Score (0-1)",
         title = paste0(wsd_source_id, "  -  combined = ", round(coastal_component_norm, 2))) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 9) +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 40, hjust = 1, size = 7),
          plot.title = element_text(size = 8, face = "bold"),
          panel.grid.major.x = element_blank())
}

contribution_plots <- coastal_full_sf %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  purrr::pmap(make_contribution_plot)

mapview(coastal_full_sf, zcol = "coastal_component_norm", col.regions = pal,
        layer.name = "Coastal component (exposure + sensitivity, combined)",
        popup = leafpop::popupGraph(contribution_plots, type = "png",
                                    width = 260, height = 220))
```
